title: Network Protocols and Role-Play Analysis

sources.title: FBLA Network Design 2026-27 Individual Guidelines
sources.scope: Read study guide pp. 6-7 for ND-NPSA objectives; pp. 2-4 for equipment and timing; p. 8 for the seven spoken rating criteria and maxima. The document leaves SMP unexplained and conflicts on flipchart/visuals.

sources.title: IETF RFC 9293: Transmission Control Protocol
sources.scope: Read the abstract and TCP service description: TCP is connection-oriented and provides reliable in-order byte-stream service; segments use IP datagrams and ports identify services.

sources.title: IETF RFC 2131: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol
sources.scope: Read DHCP overview and address-allocation/client-server sections: DHCP delivers host configuration and allocates addresses through client-server exchanges and leases; relay agents can pass requests across subnets.

sources.title: Cisco: Configure IP Addresses and Unique Subnets
sources.scope: Read network-mask/subnet sections and device terminology for IP addressing, router interfaces, and gateway relationships. Its classful framing is older; these notes do not teach classful masks as current practice.

pages.title: Network Scale and Work Models
notes: A LAN links devices within a limited local site.
A WAN connects distant LANs over carrier or private links.
WAN reach adds provider, latency, recurring-cost tradeoffs.
Peer-to-peer hosts share directly; control is distributed.
P2P can suit small groups but complicates consistent policy.
Client-server centralizes services, identity, administration.
Central services simplify control but become dependencies.
Thin clients rely on remote compute/apps; outages impair use.
Servers provide services; clients request services.

pages.title: Devices and Trust Boundaries
notes: A modem adapts a carrier access signal; products vary.
A router forwards IP packets between networks using routes.
A switch forwards local frames using learned MAC addresses.
Servers attach to switches; clients reach services over links.
An access point bridges Wi-Fi clients to a wired LAN.
A gateway joins networks or systems; roles may be combined.
A switch is not automatically a router or policy firewall.
Authentication checks an identity claim or credential control.
Authorization decides permitted actions after identity checks.
Encryption protects confidentiality when keys are secure.

pages.title: Connectivity and Attack Patterns
notes: Ethernet (IEEE 802.3) commonly carries wired LAN frames.
Wi-Fi (802.11) uses radio; walls and noise affect links.
Wi-Fi reach and rate depend on band, load, and equipment.
Bluetooth is short-range personal-area radio, not WAN access.
Phishing tricks people into unsafe disclosure or actions.
Spoofing falsifies an address or identity signal to mislead.
Poisoning corrupts trusted data, e.g. name-resolution answers.
Attack labels overlap; identify the mechanism and target.
Verify requests; use MFA, filtering, and updates.

pages.title: VPN and Authorized Capture
notes: A VPN creates a logical tunnel across an underlying network.
Configured VPNs can authenticate peers and encrypt traffic.
Tunneling does not secure endpoints or grant user permissions.
Packet capture records traffic visible at the capture point.
Encryption hides payload; metadata may remain visible.
Capture only with explicit authorization and approved scope.
Minimize collection; protect files; follow retention policy.
Authentication checks identity; authorization grants access.
VPNs do not replace endpoint, account, or network controls.
Never inspect others' traffic without authorization.

practice.prompt: A small firm has two distant offices. What makes a WAN useful, and what tradeoffs should be compared?
practice.answer: A WAN connects the offices' LANs over distance. Compare provider cost, latency, service availability, security controls, and support needs; do not assume a WAN is one specific technology.

practice.prompt: Why does an encrypted VPN not by itself authorize every connected user?
practice.answer: Encryption protects traffic in transit and peer authentication checks a tunnel endpoint; user authorization separately determines which actions/resources an identity may access.

pages.title: Layers and Addressing Roles
notes: OSI 1 physical: signaling, media, connectors, and bits.
OSI 2 data link: local frames and link-layer addressing.
OSI 3 network: IP addressing and routing between networks.
OSI 4 transport: process delivery, ports, and TCP or UDP.
OSI 5 session: coordinates dialogues between apps.
OSI 6 presentation: data representation and transformations.
OSI 7 application: network services used by applications.
OSI is a learning model; implementations may span layers.
TCP/IP names a protocol suite, not one individual protocol.

pages.title: TCP, UDP, DHCP, and Printed SMP
notes: TCP provides reliable, ordered byte-stream service.
TCP sequence numbers and ACKs support ordered recovery.
UDP has no TCP delivery or ordering guarantees.
Applications select transport to fit their requirements.
DHCP client-server exchanges configure hosts.
DHCP leases assign addresses temporarily; clients renew them.
DHCP relays pass requests to servers on other subnets.
DHCP does not establish that a device is trusted.
The guide prints SMP but leaves its meaning undefined.
Keep SMP unresolved; do not silently replace the term.

pages.title: Topology and Reachability Tests
notes: Star links devices through a center; its failure affects many.
A star cable fault usually isolates its attached endpoint.
Bus shares a backbone; a break may affect many devices.
Ring forwards around a loop; recovery depends on protection.
Physical cabling shape may differ from logical topology.
Ping tests ICMP echo; loss is evidence, not a cause.
Firewalls may block echo even when application service works.
Tracert shows responding hops; filtering can hide responses.
A hop timeout alone does not prove destination failure.

pages.title: Layered Physical Diagnosis
notes: First scope impact: one device, site, service, or all users?
Check power, cables, link lights, and Wi-Fi association.
Confirm correct SSID, enabled adapter, signal, and wired port.
Check VLAN, IP address, mask, gateway, and DNS next.
Compare gateway, permitted remote IP, then a DNS name.
IP works but names fail? Check the resolver path.
No lease suggests DHCP checks, not a proven cause.
Change one safe variable; preserve before/after evidence.
Repeat the test; document cause and outcome.
Only test cables or capture traffic when authorized and safe.

practice.prompt: A device has a valid IP and can reach a server by address but not by name. What would you test next?
practice.answer: Check configured DNS resolver and name lookup path, since IP reachability works while name resolution fails. Confirm with permitted lookup tests; this is evidence for a DNS issue, not proof until verified.

practice.prompt: Contrast a ping failure with a traceroute hop timeout. Does either prove an outage?
practice.answer: No. Ping can be filtered, and intermediate traceroute hops may not respond while forwarding traffic. Corroborate with authorized end-to-end service tests and local physical checks.

sheets.title: Analyze and Recommend a Network Design

pages.title: Define the Problem and Criteria
notes: Restate the scenario accurately before proposing technology.
Separate observed symptoms from business problems and impact.
Identify stakeholders, sites, users, data, and deadlines.
Separate stated facts, assumptions, unknowns, and risks.
Measure goals: uptime, latency, cost, or security.
Rank mandatory constraints above preferences and explain why.
Map clients, switches, servers, gateways, and WAN links.
Identify trust boundaries and single points of failure.
Use network knowledge to explain impact and constraints.

pages.title: Compare Real Alternatives
notes: Offer at least two credible options that meet the stated need.
Compare options against the same weighted decision criteria.
Assess capital, recurring cost, labor, and support effort.
Assess speed, resilience, security, complexity, and growth.
Name each option's concrete advantage and material drawback.
VPN offers control; managed WAN may simplify support.
VPN also needs endpoint, identity, and failover management.
Reject options against constraints, not straw-man comparisons.
Label estimates; avoid invented vendor guarantees.
Choose an option and acknowledge its residual risks.

pages.title: Plan Feasible Implementation
notes: Phase work: discover, design, pilot, migrate, verify, review.
Name owner, sequence, dependencies, and approval path.
List labor, equipment, licenses, circuits, and training.
Schedule maintenance and notify affected stakeholders.
Export configs and protect backups before production changes.
Set rollback trigger, owner, and tested recovery procedure.
Use least privilege, authentication, updates, and encryption.
Test access, service performance, recovery, and failover.
Compare test results with scenario success criteria.

pages.title: Connect Design to Business Value
notes: VLANs separate teams; verify routing and access rules.
Switch ACLs limit flows; test allowed and denied paths.
A second link helps only with sufficiently independent paths.
Redundancy costs more and cannot ensure app recovery.
A pilot limits impact and reveals compatibility problems.
Monitoring checks health; assign a response owner.
Document topology, configs, dependencies, and support handoff.
State decision, next action, owner, and review date.
Tie technical choices to business needs or constraints.
If key facts are unknown, propose discovery before commitment.

practice.prompt: A two-site firm needs resilient access to a central app. Compare two approaches and give a decision criterion.
practice.answer: Compare site-to-site VPN over Internet with a managed WAN. VPN may lower circuit cost but requires tunnel, endpoint, and failover management; managed WAN may simplify operations but costs more and depends on provider terms. Compare measured availability, cost, latency, and support capacity before selecting.

practice.prompt: What makes a network implementation plan feasible rather than just a preferred design?
practice.answer: It assigns owners and sequence, identifies labor/equipment/licenses, approvals and outage window, protects configuration backups, defines acceptance tests and rollback triggers, and accounts for operational support.

pages.title: Organize a Decision Briefing
notes: National format: 20 minutes prep, 7 minutes delivery.
No separate Q&A; judges may interrupt during delivery.
Sequence: problem, criteria, options, choice, implementation.
Summarize facts and prioritized problems before solutions.
Compare options' pros and cons against common criteria.
Explain how the choice meets ranked requirements.
State phases, resources, owners, tests, and rollback triggers.
Use signposts and transitions to clarify the reasoning.
Close with success measure, requested decision, and next step.

pages.title: Communicate with Confidence
notes: Project voice at a measured pace; pause after key decisions.
Use poised posture, purposeful gestures, and eye contact.
Define acronyms; connect technical terms to business impact.
Avoid jargon lists; explain mechanisms behind your choice.
Split speaking roles only when transitions stay coherent.
Every teammate should know the recommendation and risks.
Label assumptions and estimates; do not invent scenario facts.
Do not bluff when uncertain; describe safe verification steps.
Keep material explanations usable without visual aids.
Pause after key points; do not rush the conclusion.

pages.title: Answer Judges Completely
notes: Listen through the full question before answering.
Clarify scope if needed, then answer the question directly.
Support the answer with reasoning and scenario evidence.
Address each part; state limits and residual risk honestly.
For unknown facts, name what to verify and how to verify it.
If a judge challenges an assumption, reassess it calmly.
Correct factual errors plainly; return to decision logic.
Acknowledge interruption; return to your planned sequence.
Complete interaction requires reasoning, not memorized lines.

pages.title: Rubric and Practice Boundaries
notes: Maxima: problem 10; alternatives 20; solution 20.
Knowledge 20; organization, delivery, answers 10 each.
Spoken rubric totals 100 points before penalties.
Judges ask during presentation; no separate Q&A is scheduled.
Guide p.2 lists easel; p.4 prohibits visuals and props.
Conflict unresolved; ask adviser for clarification.
Do not assume permission; prepare a verbal explanation.
Practice cases are hypothetical, not official prompts.
Competitors author their own competition response.
Score rehearsal against each criterion's actual point maximum.

practice.prompt: During a hypothetical clinic Wi-Fi case, a judge asks how you know access-point placement is the cause. Respond completely.
practice.answer: It is not yet established. I would compare coverage and interference measurements in affected and unaffected rooms at peak times, review client association and wired backhaul, then pilot a placement change and repeat the same tests. I would retain rollback if performance or security worsens.

practice.prompt: Name all seven role-play criteria and their current maximum points.
practice.answer: Problem definition 10, alternatives and pros/cons 20, solution and implementation 20, event knowledge 20, organization 10, delivery 10, and judge interaction/answers 10; total 100.

lab.title: Authorized tabletop and timed decision rehearsal
steps: On paper, map a hypothetical two-site LAN/WAN with clients, switches, router, and server; predict the path to an application.
For a fictional intermittent link, state observations, assumptions, and a safe sequence of physical, IP, and service checks. Do not capture live traffic.
Compare two hypothetical connectivity designs using cost, availability, security, support, and latency; label all invented figures as exercise assumptions.
Run a 20-minute preparation and 7-minute presentation rehearsal; have a teammate interrupt with questions about evidence, rollback, cost, and security.
Score the response on all seven current rubric criteria and revise the weakest reasoning area.
expected: Learner distinguishes LAN/WAN scope and correctly traces client, switch, router, and server roles.
Learner separates facts from hypotheses and chooses non-destructive, authorized checks.
Learner explains concrete tradeoffs and a feasible phased recommendation with resources and rollback.
Learner answers each judge question with a direct claim, reason, evidence, and limitation or verification step.
Learner identifies all rubric maxima accurately and treats practice as hypothetical, not a confidential prompt.

limitations: The National guide prints SMP as an example but does not define it. This module preserves the ambiguity and does not substitute SMTP, SNMP, or another protocol; seek adviser clarification on expected scope.
Network Design guideline p.2 lists flipchart/easel while p.4 prohibits visuals and props. The conflict is unresolved here; ask the adviser and do not assume equipment permission.
